GIS Project | Greater Sydney, New South Wales | 2015–2025 | M. Marshall & T. Powell

The Wild West? Mapping Crime and Socioeconomic Patterns Across Greater Sydney



A GIS Analysis of Crime Hotspots and Socioeconomic Factors

Molly Marshall & Tara Powell

Content Warning:

Whilst nothing is explicitly described, this project discusses, explores and names a wide range of criminal offences. Many of these offences (particually those classified under Violent Crime) are confronting and may be upsetting for some readers/viewers.

If you have experienced violence or sexual assault and need immediate or ongoing help, contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) to talk to a counsellor from the national sexual assault and domestic violence hotline. For confidential support and information, contact Safe Steps’ 24/7 family violence response line on 1800 015 188.

If you have concerns about your safety or that of someone else, please contact the police in your state or territory, or call Triple Zero (000) for emergency help.

Crime does not occur uniformly across cities. Understanding where offences are concentrated, and how these patterns vary between communities, can help reveal important spatial differences in public safety (Rosser et al., 2017). Geographic Information Systems (GIS) provide tools to map these patterns, identify crime hotspots and investigate how crime rates vary across different areas.



Figure 1:A photograph of Sydney police car Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPsome

How does the spatial distribution of crime (drug offences, violent crime and property offences) vary across NSW LGAs, and to what extent is crime rate associated with unemployment, income and high-school completion?

Map recorded crime counts and rates, examining how they vary across Greater Sydney.

📍

Hotspot analysis to identify and visualise locations with high concentrations of recorded offences.

📊

Explore associations between socioeconomic factors, unemployment, income and education, and crime rates.

🔎
Use GIS workflows in Python to investigate geographic patterns.

This project uses GIS to investigate the spatial distribution of recorded crime across selected Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Greater Sydney between 2015 and 2025. It identifies areas with higher concentrations of crime and explores whether crime rates are associated with socioeconomic characteristics, including unemployment, weekly household income and high-school completion.

The relationship between crime and socioeconomic conditions is important when examining differences in crime rates between urban areas. Weatherburn (1992) explores the relationship between economic adversity and crime, while Walker and Henderson (1991) discuss Australian crime trends and the importance of considering social and demographic factors when interpreting crime statistics. Together, these studies highlight the value of examining socioeconomic conditions alongside geographic crime patterns.

Sharma and Tailor (2023) further demonstrate the value of spatial analysis by investigating crime hotspots and urban characteristics in Surat, India. Their research compares spatial interpolation techniques and examines associations between crime, land use and road connectivity. Although their findings relate to a different urban context, the study highlights the importance of appropriate GIS methods when investigating spatial crime patterns. Further studies also demonstrate the value of GIS for identifying crime hotspots. Ansari and Kale (2014), in their study of Aurangabad City, used techniques including Kernel Density Estimation (KDE), Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) and Getis-Ord Gi* to identify concentrations of criminal activity. Similarly, Chainey, Tompson and Uhlig (2008) compared different crime hotspot mapping techniques, highlighting the importance of selecting appropriate methods for identifying spatial crime patterns. These studies provide a foundation for using GIS to investigate crime hotspots across Greater Sydney.

Crime trends in New South Wales (NSW) have changed considerably over recent decades, with long-term declines in many property offences and a more complex pattern of change in violent crime. Payne (2025) revisits the widely documented NSW crime decline and demonstrates that findings can be influenced by changes in data-matching methods and the way young people are processed through the criminal justice system. More recent statistics show that, across Greater Sydney, violent offences increased by an average of 2.1% annually over the ten years to June 2025, while property offences declined by an average of 3.0% annually (BOCSAR, 2025). High-profile violent incidents in Sydney have also drawn attention to how crime is understood and represented publicly. Tomkinson and Harper (2025) examine how the Bondi Junction and Wakeley stabbing attacks in April 2024 were framed differently within media and political discourse, particularly in relation to gender-based violence and ideological extremism. Their research highlights how media and political narratives can shape the public understanding and interpretation of violent crime, demonstrating the importance of considering how crime is represented alongside its recorded patterns. Together, these studies highlight the importance of examining different crime categories separately and considering both changes over time and differences between locations. This provides context for investigating the spatial distribution of drug, violent and property offences across Greater Sydney LGAs and their associations with socioeconomic characteristics.

By combining crime data with socioeconomic information, this project aims to provide a clearer picture of how crime patterns vary geographically. Specifically, it explores the spatial distribution of crime and whether differences in crime rates correspond with variations in unemployment, household income and high-school completion. These relationships are examined as spatial associations rather than evidence that socioeconomic conditions directly cause crime.

GIS Project | Greater Sydney, New South Wales | 2015–2025 | M. Marshall & T. Powell

The study area for this project is the Greater Sydney Region, New South Wales (NSW), Australia. This region was selected due to the availability of sufficient crime data and socioeconomic statistics to support spatial and statistical analysis. 30 LGAs across the Greater Sydney area were selected for the analysis and can be seen in Figure 1. The study examines crime patterns across Local Government Areas (LGAs) between 2015 and 2025, focusing on drug offences, violent crime and property offences. The analysis explores the spatial distribution of crime and its relationship with unemployment, median income and high-school completion rates.

Figure 1:Locality Map of the Local Government Areas (LGA) of Greater Sydney that were used in this project

Three primary datasets were used to investigate the spatial and socioeconomic distribution of crime across selected Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Greater Sydney between January 2015 and December 2025. Crime incident data were obtained from the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR), LGA boundary data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), and socioeconomic indicators from the 2021 Australian Census.

The datasets were cleaned, aggregated and integrated into a common spatial dataset to enable comparisons between crime patterns and socioeconomic characteristics. The following tables summarise the source data, file formats and their roles in the analysis.

The following sections provide further details of the data preparation, socioeconomic statistical analysis and spatial hotspot analysis. Expand each section to explore the methodology.DATA COLLECTION AND PREPARATION

Data Collection and Preparation

Data sources

Three primary datasets were used in this study:

Dataset

Source

Purpose

Local Government Areas (2025)

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)

Provided polygon geometries and geographic identifiers for the 30 selected LGAs.

Recorded Criminal Incidents by Month by LGA

NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR)

Provided monthly recorded crime counts for 2015–2025.

2021 Census General Community Profile G01, G02 & G43

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)

Provided socioeconomic indicators for education, household income and labour force characteristics.

Crime classification

Recorded offences were grouped into three categories:

Drug offences: Possession, dealing, manufacturing and importing.

Violent crime: Abduction and kidnapping, assault, coercive control, homicide, intimidation, stalking and harassment, sexual offences, and robbery.

Property offences: Theft, arson and malicious damage to property.

Data preparation

Python was used to clean and integrate the datasets.

The following libaries were used during this project:import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plot
from scipy import stats

The workflow involved:

Selecting the 30 study-area LGAs using their geographic identifiers.

Filtering crime records to the selected LGAs and relevant offence categories.

Aggregating monthly crime records into annual counts for 2015 - 2025.

Extracting the relevant socioeconomic indicators from the 2021 Census.

Joining crime and socioeconomic attributes to the LGA polygons using matching geographic identifiers.

Checking for missing values, inconsistent identifiers and invalid geometries.

The resulting spatial dataset:SydneyLGAs_MGA202056_socioecon_crime_2015_2025.shp

provided a consistent geographic framework for mapping crime, calculating rates, identifying hotspots and examining socioeconomic associations.SPATIAL ANALYSIS

Spatial Analysis

Crime Counts

Total recorded incidents were calculated for each LGA and crime category across 2015–2025 by summing the annual recorded crime counts over the study period. These totals were used to compare the overall count and spatial distribution of drug offences, violent crime and property offences.

Crime Rates

Crime rates were calculated to account for differences in population size between LGAs, allowing for more meaningful comparisons of crime levels across the study area.\text{Crime rate} = 
\frac{\text{Total recorded incidents (2015–2025)}} 
{\text{Population denominator}} 
\times 1000

This measure expresses recorded incidents per 1,000 residents over the study period for each LGA.

The resulting spatial dataset:SydneyLGAs_SpatialCrimeAnalysis.shp

contained both crime rate and counts for each LGA and was used for visualisation of these results.

Getis–Ord Gi Hotspot Analysis*

The Getis–Ord statistics were used to examine the spatial concentration of crime rates across the selected LGAs. The analysis included the Global Getis–Ord (G) statistic, which measures overall spatial concentration, and the Local Getis–Ord (G_i^*) statistic, which identifies individual LGAs forming clusters of high or low crime-rate values.

The analysis was conducted in Python uisng PySAL. The following libaries were used during the hotpsot analysis:from esda.getisord import G
from esda.getisord import G_Local
from libpysal import weights

Two statistics were computed per crime type (violent crime, property offences and drug offences):

Global Getis–Ord G

The Global Getis–Ord (G) statistic measures whether high or low values are spatially concentrated across the study area. The observed (G) statistic is compared with its expected value under spatial randomness. A Z-score and p-value are then used to assess whether the observed spatial concentration is statistically significant.

Local Getis–Ord (G_i^*)

The Local Getis–Ord (G_i^*) statistic identifies individual LGAs where crime rates are spatially clustered. It considers the value of the focal LGA and the values of its neighbouring LGAs.

The analysis used:

Input variables: Crime rates per 1,000 residents for drug offences, violent crime and property offences.

Spatial weights: Queen contiguity, where LGAs are neighbours if their polygons share an edge or vertex. Binary spatial weights assigned a value of 1 to neighbouring LGAs and 0 to non-neighbouring LGAs.

Statistics: Both Global Getis–Ord G and Local Getis–Ord Gi* statistics were calculated. Global G assessed the overall spatial concentration of crime rates across the study area, while Local Gi* identified individual LGAs with clusters of high or low values.

Permutations: 199 permutations were used for the Local Gi* analysis because larger permutation counts caused computational problems (computer used did not have enough processing capcity). A fixed random seed of 12345 was used to support reproducibility.

Significance threshold: (p < 0.05), using permutation-based p-values for the Local Gi* analysis.

Classification: LGAs were classified as hotspots, coldspots or not statistically significant based on their Local Gi* Z-scores and p-values.

The Local (G_i^*) analysis was performed separately for drug offences, violent crime and property offences, using crime rates per 1,000 residents. Statistical significance was assessed using 199 permutations, a fixed random seed of 12345 and a threshold of (p < 0.05). The Global (G) statistic used an analytical normal approximation to calculate its Z-score and p-value.

LGAs with statistically significant positive Local (G_i^*) Z-scores were classified as hotspots, indicating clusters of relatively high crime rates. LGAs with statistically significant negative Z-scores were classified as coldspots, indicating clusters of relatively low crime rates. LGAs that did not meet the significance threshold were classified as not statistically significant. The resulting classifications were mapped to compare spatial patterns across the three crime categories.

The resulting spatial dataset:SydneyLGAs_GetisOrd.shp

was used for visualisation of the hotspot results.SOCIOECON ANALYSIS

Socioeconomic Statistical Analysis

The socioeconomic analysis investigated associations between crime and four indicators: time, year 12 completion in the adult population, household income and unemployment.

Socioeconomic indicators

Education: Highest year of school completed, Year 12 or equivalent, sourced from 2021 Census Table G01.

Household income: Median total weekly household income, sourced from 2021 Census Table G02.

Unemployment: Selected labour force statistics, sourced from 2021 Census Table G43.

Percentage Computation

High-school completion and unemployment percentages were calculated for each LGA using data from the 2021 Australian Census. High-school completion was calculated by dividing the number of people whose highest year of school completion was Year 12 or equivalent by the total population aged 20 years and over, then multiplying by 100. The population aged 20 years and over was calculated by summing the Census age groups from 20–24 years to 85 years and over.\text{High-school completion (\%)} =
\frac{\text{People with Year 12 completion}}
{\text{Population aged 20 years and over}}
\times 100

Unemployment percentage was calculated by dividing the number of unemployed people looking for work by the total labour force, then multiplying by 100. The total labour force was used as the denominator rather than the total population, as this measure relates to people participating in the labour force rather than the entire population, which includes children.\text{Unemployment (\%)} =
\frac{\text{Unemployed people looking for work}}
{\text{Total labour force}}
\times 100

The calculated percentages and median weekly household income were joined to the LGA polygon dataset using matching geographic identifiers, allowing the socioeconomic indicators to be mapped and compared with crime patterns across the study area.

Analytical approach

The socioeconomic indicators were compared with drug offences, violent crime and property offences to investigate potential relationships between socioeconomic conditions and crime. The socioeconomic variables represent conditions recorded at the 2021 Census, while crime data span 2015–2025. Pearson’s correlation coefficient is a value between -1 and 1 which quantifies how linear the relationship between 2 variables is. The signifigance threshold was a p value of 0.05. Pearson’s correlation coefficent represents assosiations between datasets, not nessesarily causation.

The analysis considered:

Associations between socioeconomic characteristics and crime rates across the selected LGAs.

Relationships between changes in annual crime rates and time within individual LGAs.

Socioeconomic Correlation Analysis

Pearson’s correlation coeffcient was calculated for each crime type (rate per 1000 people for each LGA) and each socioeconomic variable (for each LGA) resulting in r and p values.

Time Correlation Analysis

Annual crime rates from 2015–2025 were plotted for individual LGAs to examine changes over time. SciPy was used to perform a Least Squares Analysis on the dataset to determine a linear (first order) line of best fit for the dataset. The slope value of this line of best fit was used to quantify the rate of change over time. Statistical significance was assessed using a threshold of (p < 0.05). LGAs which did not have a statistically signifigant change in crime rate over time were given a rate of change over time value of 0.

The resulting spatial dataset:SydneyLGAs_MGA202056_socioecon_crime_2015_2025.shp

contained the relevant values and percentages for the three socioeconomic factorsMAPS AND GRAPHS

Results Visualisation

Web Maps

Three interactive web maps were developed using Python and the Leafmap library to explore and communicate the spatial distribution of crime and its relationship with socioeconomic characteristics across Greater Sydney LGAs. The maps were developed using the streamlit-map-template (

https://​github​.com​/opengeos​/streamlit​-map​-template) repository by OpenGeo, which provided the base template for the web applications. Leafmap was used to create the interactive maps and display the spatial datasets. Each map was published as an individual web application using Streamlit by connecting the relevant Python script from our GitHub repository.

Python was used to create the map web code and the following libaries were imported during the creation of the web maps:import streamlit as st
import leafmap.foliumap as leafmap
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from folium.plugins import MeasureControl

The following three web maps were created:

Crime counts and rates: The first map displayed recorded crime counts and crime rates per 1,000 residents for drug offences, violent crime and property offences. This allowed users to compare the count and population-adjusted distribution of each crime category across LGAs.

Crime hotspots: The second map displayed the Local Getis–Ord Gi* hotspot classifications for each crime category, distinguishing hotspots, coldspots and areas that were not statistically significant. This enabled comparisons of spatial clustering patterns between crime types.

Crime trends and socioeconomic characteristics: The third map explored recorded crime trends across Greater Sydney LGAs from 2015 to 2025. Interactive pop-ups displayed socioeconomic indicator values for each LGA from the 2021 Census, including household income, unemployment and high school completion rate. This allowed users to explore changes in crime alongside the socioeconomic characteristics of each area.

Graphs

Python was used to create all graphs using the following libaries:import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plot

Graphs were used to examine relationships between crime rates and socioeconomic indicators, including household income, unemployment and high-school completion. Additional time-series graphs illustrated changes in crime rates between 2015 and 2025, allowing comparisons between LGAs and investigation of trends within selected areas.

Map Highlights

Overall, crime counts tend to be lower in the northern LGAs, while higher counts are observed across southern and western LGAs. This spatial pattern is consistent across all three crime categories.

A similar pattern is evident in crime rates, with northern LGAs generally recording lower rates than those in the southern and western parts of the study area.

Sydney LGA presents the highest crime count for drug offences

Blacktown LGA presents the highest crime count for violent crime and property offences, However, Sydney LGA presnts the highest crime rate for all crime types

Map 2: Interactive crime trends map of Greater Sydney

Map Highlights

Blacktown, Paramatta and Burwood all have increasing drug offences over time. All other LGA’s have decreasing drug offences or no correlation over time

Majority of LGA’s, except Sydney, Hunters Hill, Mosman and North Sydney, have increasing violent crime over time

Majority of LGA’s, except Strathfield, Camden, Parramatta, Ryde and Lane Cove, have decreasing property offences over time

Drug offences: The Global Getis–Ord G statistic was statistically significant (G=0.1707, p=0.0401). The observed value exceeded the expected value, indicating evidence of an overall spatial concentration of high drug-offence rates.

Violent crime: Violent crime showed the strongest statistical evidence of spatial concentration (G=0.1580, Z=2.2041, p=0.0138). The result suggests that violent crime rates were more spatially concentrated than expected under spatial randomness.

Property offences: The result was not statistically significant (G=0.1433, p=0.0913). Although the observed statistic exceeded the expected value, there was insufficient evidence at the 0.05 significance level to conclude that property-offence rates displayed significant overall spatial concentration.
